old_entry.title: Air Traffic Controller
old_entry.summary: Air Traffic Controller is a video game written by air traffic controller David Mannering.
body: Air Traffic Controller is a video game written by air traffic controller David Mannering. It was released by Creative Computing for the TRS-80 Model I and Exidy Sorcerer in 1978, and for the Apple II and Sol-20 in 1979. It was  rewritten by Will Fastie and Bill Appelbaum for Data General AOS in 1980 and ported to MS-DOS for release by PC Disk Magazine in 1983.
An enhanced version, Advanced Air Traffic Controller, was published by Creative Computing in 1981 for the TRS-80, Apple II, Commodore PET, and Atari 8-bit computers.
Air Traffic Controller is a game in which the player directs local air traffic.
Alan Isabelle reviewed Air Traffic Controller in The Space Gamer, commenting that it was "Unquestionably worth [the price]. I highly recommend this to anyone with the computer to run it.".

old_entry.title: Adventure
old_entry.subtitle: A small kingdom and a hidden signature
old_entry.summary: Warren Robinett translated exploration into rooms, coloured shapes and a secret author credit.
body: Atari's Adventure adapted ideas from text adventures to a joystick-controlled world. A square hero could carry objects between rooms, unlock passages and encounter dragons. Its economical shapes asked the player to remember connections across a larger space.

Robinett also concealed a room bearing his name, making a now-famous argument for recognising the people who create games. The secret is a reminder that authorship was not always visible on a box or title screen.

editorial_features.title: Keeping the makers' names
editorial_features.summary: A hidden signature and a shared list record human work.
body: Warren Robinett called the name hidden in Adventure his signature. In a 2015 interview, he described keeping it secret because it could otherwise have been removed before the cartridges were manufactured. Once copies had travelled into homes, the name could no longer be removed from them. He remembered explaining the trick to former Atari colleagues over pizza after leaving the company. The concealed room carried an argument about recognition, but its survival also depended on timing, secrecy and the physical distribution of software.

Robinett's memories also name people around the work who rarely fit the image of a solitary programmer. Steve Harding, who wrote Atari manuals, played unfinished games and offered feedback. Later, Robinett founded The Learning Company with Ann McCormick Piestrup, Leslie Grimm and Teri Perl, who wanted to make learning games. He recalled initially having his name on that company's packaging and later losing it. A surviving credit could reveal one contribution while leaving others harder to recover. Remembering a production meant asking who tested, taught, wrote and collaborated.

The IGDA's March 2023 crediting guide moved the problem into the production schedule. Its committee proposed agreeing on rules early and treating the credits as a feature with work to complete. Contractors and outside vendors belonged in that conversation, with individual workers' names collected rather than only a company label. Team members should have time to review their proposed entries before release. Behind the familiar scrolling list was a process of gathering information, checking roles and making space for the people whose work had crossed organisational boundaries.

The same guide considered what happens when the team changes. It recommended informing departing contributors about their credits, maintaining records for ongoing games and correcting mistakes through the bug process. A missing name or wrong role could be a defect to fix in a later update. These proposals made recognition an activity that continued beyond a launch deadline. Someone had to keep the list, preserve changes and listen when contributors found errors. The historical record emerged through ordinary production decisions, one entry at a time.

old_entry.title: Koei
old_entry.subtitle: Koei Turns History into a System to Manage
old_entry.summary: On July 25, 1978 Yōichi and Keiko Erikawa founded Koei.
body: On July 25, 1978 Yōichi and Keiko Erikawa founded Koei. Before becoming one of the most recognizable names in Japanese strategy games, the company worked with computers and business software. From that familiarity with data and systems emerged, during the 1980s, a catalog able to treat history as a set of resources, territories, officers and decisions. Nobunaga's Ambition and Romance of the Three Kingdoms built a tradition lasting decades, while other projects broadened its audience. Koei's history shows how business-computing expertise could become video game grammar.

Yoichi and Keiko Erikawa found Koei in 1978, before the company becomes synonymous with large historical strategy games. Its shift from computer and software work to entertainment takes place on machines suited to storing information, performing calculations and presenting choices. These qualities are less immediately striking than arcade graphics, but crucial to the company's direction. A campaign can make victory depend on harvests, budgets and the balance of power rather than reflexes. This helps explain why computers become a creative environment for Koei: they make complex systems playable without requiring players to carry out all the administrative work those systems would demand on paper.

Beginning in 1983, Nobunaga's Ambition turns Japan's Sengoku period into a territory to administer as well as conquer. Later entries expand the model, but the relationship between land and resources remains central: an army needs an economic base, and military gains must be sustainable. Players therefore see conflict through the responsibilities of government. Attacking immediately does not always mean making progress, since it can leave other needs unattended. History supplies names, geography and rivalries; simulation allows their outcomes to change. The result is not a prescribed lesson to repeat, but a set of conditions on which the player can act.

Romance of the Three Kingdoms, launched in 1985, brings Koei's strategy design to the China of the celebrated historical novel. Territory matters, but government also depends on people: recruiting officers, assigning responsibilities and retaining their loyalty become part of building power. Characters' abilities make relationships a resource distinct from money or soldiers. Across changing perspectives and systems, the series retains this connection between administration and individual lives. The past becomes something players can renegotiate. Its protagonists remain recognizable, while alliances and decisions can lead a campaign away from the sequence of events a reader already knows.
